exercises.prompt: All flurbs are wobbles. No wobble is a zant. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
exercises.explanation: Every flurb is a wobble, and no wobble is a zant, so no flurb can be a zant either — a chain of "all" into "no" transfers cleanly.

exercises.prompt: A plane mirror flips your reflection left-to-right (raise your right hand, the reflection raises what looks like its left) but never flips it upside-down. Why does a mirror swap left and right but not up and down? Work out the explanation, then reveal and compare.
exercises.answer: A mirror actually reverses front-to-back (depth), not left-right; the apparent left-right swap happens because we imagine rotating ourselves around a vertical axis to face the same way as our reflection, and that rotation is what swaps left and right.
exercises.explanation: The mirror only inverts the axis perpendicular to its surface (front-to-back). There's no physical left-right flip at all — the illusion comes from mentally rotating yourself to compare orientations, and a vertical-axis rotation is what puts left and right on opposite sides.

exercises.prompt: A famous flawed "proof by induction" claims all horses are the same color. Base case: a group of just 1 horse is trivially all one color. Inductive step: assume any group of $n$ horses is all one color; given a group of $n+1$ horses, remove one horse to get an $n$-horse group (all one color by assumption), then swap which horse was removed to get a different $n$-horse group (also all one color) — the two groups overlap, so all $n+1$ horses share that color. Where exactly does this argument break down?
choices: The inductive step fails specifically going from $n=1$ to $n=2$: two single-horse groups don't overlap, so there's no shared horse linking them.
The base case is false, since a single horse isn't guaranteed to be one color.
The claim is actually true; there is no flaw.
Induction cannot be used to reason about colors at all.
exercises.answer: The inductive step fails specifically going from $n=1$ to $n=2$: two single-horse groups don't overlap, so there's no shared horse linking them.
exercises.explanation: For $n \ge 2$, two overlapping $n$-subsets of an $(n+1)$-group always share at least one horse, linking their colors. That breaks precisely at $n=1$: two single-horse groups of a 2-horse set share no horse, so nothing forces them to match.

exercises.prompt: Two piles of stones sit on the table: one with 3 stones, one with 5. On each turn, a player removes any positive number of stones from exactly one pile (their choice which pile, and how many). Whoever takes the last stone wins. You move first — which move guarantees you a win?
choices: Take 2 stones from the 5-stone pile, leaving 3 and 3.
Take all 3 stones from the smaller pile, leaving 0 and 5.
Take 1 stone from the 3-stone pile, leaving 2 and 5.
It doesn't matter — the second player always wins from 3 and 5.
exercises.answer: Take 2 stones from the 5-stone pile, leaving 3 and 3.
exercises.explanation: This is Nim: a position is losing for the player about to move exactly when the pile sizes XOR to 0. $3 \oplus 5 = 6 \neq 0$, so the first player wins by moving to an XOR-0 position — equalizing the piles at $3, 3$ — after which mirroring the opponent's every move guarantees the last stone.

exercises.prompt: A factory's widgets come from two machines. Machine A makes 70% of all widgets and 2% of its output is defective. Machine B makes the remaining 30% and 8% of its output is defective. A widget is picked at random and found defective. What is the probability (rounded to the nearest whole percent) that it came from Machine B?
exercises.explanation: $P(B \cap \text{def}) = 0.3 \times 0.08 = 0.024$ and $P(A \cap \text{def}) = 0.7 \times 0.02 = 0.014$, for a total defect probability of $0.038$. So $P(B \mid \text{def}) = 0.024/0.038 \approx 0.632$, or 63%.

exercises.prompt: Starting at point A, you walk 5 km east, then 3 km north, then 5 km west. How far are you from point A now, and in which direction?
exercises.explanation: The 5 km east and 5 km west legs cancel exactly, leaving only the 3 km north displacement.
